items.title: Prozac in veterans: one small trial, and mixed results since
items.where: C. The "Hardened" Circuit: Dynorphin & DeltaFosB, P2
items.your_version: Why Standard Meds Failed You If you have tried SSRIs (antidepressants) and failed, you are not crazy. In a small trial of male combat veterans with severe, long-term PTSD, Prozac did no better than a placebo (Hertzberg, et al, 2000). Trials in veterans have been mixed since, yet the VA still recommends sertraline and paroxetine (VA/DoD, 2023). And the side effects are well-known, including anhedonia, zombification, and sexual dysfunction.

items.title: Why SSRIs fail some people: nobody knows; why ketones: a mouse finding
items.where: C. The "Hardened" Circuit: Dynorphin & DeltaFosB, P3
items.your_version: Why don't these drugs on calcified PTSD? Because even if they did work for mood by modulating serotonin transmission, PTSD is not a mood disorder. That's like a bit like putting some Bengay on a broken leg.This protocol tries to get at the underpinnings of the problem. The ketone BHB blocks enzymes called HDACs (Shimazu, et al, 2013), and in mice that couldn't hold on to extinction learning (learning that a cue is now safe), an HDAC blocker made the new learning last (Whittle & Singewald, 2014). Whether ketosis does that in people hasn't been tested.

items.title: DeltaFosB fades, slowly; what iboga and psilocybin were shown to do
items.where: C. The "Hardened" Circuit: Dynorphin & DeltaFosB, P5
items.your_version:
The Fix (The Unlock): DeltaFosB does fade on its own, but slowly, and the same fears keep making more. Along with therapy and the de-armoring supplements, we use "System Reformats" (Psychedelics and Iboga). Iboga raised GDNF, a growth factor that protects dopamine neurons, in rats (He, et al, 2005), and one dose of psilocybin grew new connections in mouse brains that lasted a month (Shao, et al, 2021). Whether either loosens DeltaFosB's hold hasn't been tested directly, although these have been shown to help with addictions, which DeltaFosB plays a role in. 

While the science is focused on some specific substances in certain psychedelics, like psilocybin and ibogaine, the reality is much more complicated. Each iboga tree and each mushroom strain (and phenotype) have different levels of different psychedelic alkaloids apart from the principle ones studied. You can learn more about the different types of iboga in [my iboga guide](iboga.u-dont-exist.com). Aside from the different ibogas, I find [loveyhuasca](soma.u-dont-exist.com) to be more clear-headed than shrooms and often more beneficial, although some shroom strains, like Orissa India, are much more therapeutic than others (like Golden Teacher, Penis Envy) in my experience. And part of the way these help, from my understanding, is their antiparasitic action. Each psychedelic, and even each mushroom strain seems to target a different subset of parasites, and there's an anecdote-based theory that physical parasites solidify mental and spiritual ones. I remember eating some B+ strain shrooms which people told me were very mild and gentle. For me it was the opposite, absolute hell, until a very large and strange parasite came out and then instantly I felt amazing. More recently, I've learned that the toxins released during the psychedelic parasite cleanse actually block a lot of the benefits that we can get from the experience. Binding those toxins or protecting the brain from them is crucial for max benefits. I explain my methods for doing so in my [Altered States Guide] (badtrips.u-dont-exist.com).

items.title: Brain fog: some regions burn less glucose in PTSD
items.where: D. The "Lagging" System: Toxicity & Hypometabolism (The Fog), P1
items.my_version: The Problem: "Brain Fog" may partly be a fuel problem. In brain scans of people with PTSD, some regions burn less glucose (sugar), and the less they burn, the worse the symptoms (Jeong, et al, 2019).
items.before: The Problem: "Brain Fog" is often a fuel crisis. Trauma causes cerebral insulin resistance--your neurons are swimming in glucose (sugar) but cannot burn it. The engine is flooded.

items.title: Ketones and PQQ, as far as they're shown; the shower sentence out
items.where: D. The "Lagging" System: Toxicity & Hypometabolism (The Fog), P2
items.my_version: The Fix: If the brain is burning less sugar, we give it another fuel. Ketones are its backup fuel, and brains that take up less glucose (as in early Alzheimer's) still take up ketones normally (Cunnane, et al, 2016). PQQ made mouse cells build more mitochondria, the parts of the cell that burn fuel (Chowanadisai, et al, 2010); whether it does that in the human brain hasn't been shown.
items.before: The Fix: If the brain cannot burn sugar, we switch fuels. We use PQQ to boost ATP, and Ketones, which bypass the broken glucose pathways and enter the mitochondria directly. This turns the lights back on immediately. We alternate hot and cold showers to boost p131 and heat shock proteins and reduce inflammation.

items.title: The Jammer: fewer flashbacks, not a permanently reduced sting
items.where: E. The "Save Button": Memory Reconsolidation, P2
items.my_version: The Fix ("The Jammer"): Memories require visual processing power to be restored. If you occupy the Visual-Spatial Working Memory (e.g., playing Tetris) during the critical window after a flashback, the brain fails to "save" the visual details as strongly, and the memory flashes back less often. In the lab, a reminder of a day-old memory followed by Tetris cut its flashbacks, and neither one alone did (James, et al, 2015).
items.before: The Fix ("The Jammer"): Memories require visual processing power to be restored. If you occupy the Visual-Spatial Working Memory (e.g., playing Tetris) during the critical window after a flashback, the brain fails to "save" the visual details. The memory is restored, but the emotional "sting" is permanently reduced.

items.title: Color-Path Connect is untested; skip verbal tasks
items.where: E. The "Save Button": Memory Reconsolidation, P3
items.my_version: Instead of Tetris (which requires app/phone), you can use the "Color-Path Connect" method. It hasn't been tested the way Tetris has, but it is built on the same idea: it makes your brain map 3D space, which competes with the visual "saving" of a traumatic memory. Skip counting and word games, though: in the lab, a verbal quiz game after a trauma film led to more flashbacks, not fewer (Holmes, et al, 2010).
